name: Mappilappattu & Vattappattu (wedding repertories)
tagline: Living Mappila wedding songs — circle sings, claps and call‑and‑response
summary: Traditional Mappila wedding‑song repertories from North Malabar: Vattappattu circle‑songs and related Mappilappattu performed on wedding eve in Malappuram district, preserved in family and school…
description: Mappilappattu (Mappila songs) is the broad Arabi‑Malayalam song tradition of Malabar; Vattappattu is the circle‑song repertory associated especially with wedding eve functions in north Malabar (Malappuram).

Sung in Arabi‑Malayalam with Tamil and Arabic influences, these songs use named ishals (melodic modes), coordinated hand‑claps (kaimuttippattu) and a fixed sequence of wedding items (munajath, virutham, salam kavi, kalyana kavi, mangalam).

Performances remain a living practice in Malappuram — sung by separate male and female groups, exchanged as call‑and‑response between the groom’s and bride’s parties, and presented both in family weddings and as a competition/teaching item at school and local festivals.

The repertory preserves poetic strains by classic and local poets and continues to adapt — taught in youth festivals and Kalolsavam programmes even as some live‑troop practices shrink with changing wedding schedules.
highlights: Circle singing with hand‑clap rhythm (no instruments in Vattappattu performances)
Call‑and‑response exchange between groom’s and bride’s singers
Structured song sequence: munajath, virutham, salam kavi, kalyana kavi, mangalam
Arabi‑Malayalam language with Tamil/Arabic poetic layers
Both a living wedding ritual and a competitive/teaching item in schools and Kalolsavams
Often performed late evening or overnight at wedding‑eve functions

sections.heading: Background
body: Mappilappattu names a wide set of Muslim folk songs from Malabar; wedding‑related subgenres (kalyanappattu, vattappattu, padappattu) have long served lifecycle functions. Vattappattu literally means 'circle song' and denotes group singing with rhythmic clapping, sometimes using simple local objects (kolambi/spittoon, fans) to mark rhythm.

Poets and oral compilers from both Tamil and Malabar traditions contribute material; historic poets and local authors sit alongside countless anonymous tunes that families and neighbourhood troupes keep alive. Scholarly projects and cultural bodies document these texts and performances while local schools continue to teach them.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: At a wedding‑eve function in Malappuram you will see two separate singer groups (bride’s side and groom’s side) form circles and exchange songs. Listen for the opening supplication (munajath), metrical verses (virutham), welcome songs (salam kavi), celebratory kalyana kavi and closing mangalam, and for the strict rule that responding singers avoid repeating the same ishal or verse.

If you cannot attend a private wedding, look for Vattappattu and Mappilappattu items at local cultural festivals, college fests and the Kerala School Kalolsavam where the form is offered as a judged competitive item — contemporary writeups confirm Vattappattu is still part of school and festival syllabi.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: These are living, mostly private wedding repertoires: approach through a local contact, community cultural group or mosque committee if you want to attend a wedding performance. Many troupes also appear at public cultural events in Malappuram district; check festival and college cultural‑fest schedules for Vattappattu entries.

If you are recording or photographing, always ask permission from hosts and performers first. For research or extended listening, contact local cultural organisations, college music departments or the Mappila heritage documentation projects that publish transcriptions and studies.

latest.text: Kerala Tourism (2026) describes Vattappattu as an active marriage‑song form in Malabar with named song sequence and poet contributions, confirming the form’s continued recognition by the state tourism department.

A practical guide for competitions notes Vattappattu remains an active judged item in contemporary Kerala school and youth festivals, showing the repertory’s living teaching role (e.g., Kerala Kalolsavam templates).

visitorInfo.bestTime: Year‑round; wedding eve functions happen throughout the year — confirm dates with local hosts or festival organisers.
visitorInfo.howToReach: Use Malappuram district as your base; reach the region by rail/air to larger hubs (Kozhikode/Calicut or nearby railway stations) and travel locally by road. Arrange a local contact to be invited to private wedding events or check festival/college‑event schedules.
etiquette: Weddings are private — get an invitation or local introduction before attending.
Ask before recording audio or video; performers and families expect respect and permission.
Dress modestly and follow local etiquette; small respectful gifts for hosts are welcome.
If researching texts or tunes, rely on local cultural organisations and published documentation rather than assuming uniform repertoire across villages.
